content: Buformin, chemically known as 1-butylbiguanide, is an oral antidiabetic medication belonging to the biguanide class. It is structurally related to metformin and phenformin. The drug was marketed under the trade name Silubin by the German pharmaceutical company Grünenthal. Buformin hydrochloride appears as a fine, white to slightly yellow crystalline powder that is odorless and has a weakly acidic, bitter taste. It has a melting point of 174 to 177°C. The compound is a strong base, freely soluble in water, methanol, and ethanol, but insoluble in chloroform and ether. Toxicity studies indicate that the subcutaneous LD50 in guinea pigs is 18 mg/kg, while the intraperitoneal LD50 in mice is 140 mg/kg, and the oral LD50 in mice is 300 mg/kg. Buformin exerts its antidiabetic effects by delaying glucose absorption in the gastrointestinal tract, enhancing insulin sensitivity, increasing glucose uptake into cells, and inhibiting hepatic glucose production. Unlike hypoglycemic agents, buformin and other biguanides are antihyperglycemic, meaning they do not induce hypoglycemia but instead reduce basal and postprandial hyperglycemia in diabetic patients. Biguanides may also counteract the action of glucagon, thereby lowering fasting glucose levels. Buformin is not absorbed in the stomach, and its serum levels and urinary elimination rates are linearly correlated. The drug is eliminated with an average half-life of 2 hours, and approximately 84% of the administered dose is excreted unchanged in the urine. Buformin is not metabolized in humans, and its oral bioavailability ranges from 40% to 60%. It exhibits minimal or no binding to plasma proteins. The recommended daily dose of buformin is 150–300 mg, administered orally. A sustained-release formulation, Silubin Retard, is still available in Romania. Common side effects of buformin include anorexia, nausea, diarrhea, a metallic taste, and weight loss. Its use is contraindicated in conditions such as diabetic coma, ketoacidosis, severe infections, trauma, renal or hepatic impairment, heart failure, recent myocardial infarction, dehydration, alcoholism, and any condition that predisposes to lactic acidosis. Buformin was withdrawn from the market in many countries due to an increased risk of lactic acidosis. However, it remains available and prescribed in Romania (as Silubin Retard, sold by Zentiva), Hungary, Taiwan, and Japan. Lactic acidosis was rare in patients with normal renal function. In one study, the toxic oral dose was reported as 329 ± 30 mg/day in 24 patients who developed lactic acidosis, while another group of 24 patients on 258 ± 25 mg/day did not develop this condition. Buformin, along with phenformin and metformin, has demonstrated anticancer properties. These drugs inhibit cancer growth by disrupting the Warburg effect, which is the reliance of cancer cells on cytosolic glycolysis. They restore normal mitochondrial oxidation of pyruvate. Metformin, in particular, reduces hepatic glucose production in diabetics and disrupts the Warburg effect in cancer cells through AMPK activation and inhibition of the mTOR pathway. Buformin was first synthesized as an oral antidiabetic agent in 1957.
